title: Framework Unveils 192 GB Desktop PC Built to Run AI Models Locally
excerpt: The compact mini-ITX system, powered by AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495, can run DeepSeek V4-Flash at Q8 quantization on a single box — no discrete GPU required.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Framework's new Desktop PC features AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 and 192 GB of LPDDR5X memory.
  • The system can run DeepSeek V4-Flash at Q8 quantization, occupying approximately 162 GB.
  • An open-ended PCIe x4 slot allows for larger PCIe cards and enhanced clustering capabilities.
  • Pricing for the new model is expected to exceed $5,000, significantly higher than the current model.

Framework has previewed an upgraded version of its compact Desktop PC, now powered by AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 processor and equipped with 192 GB of unified LPDDR5X memory. The system, shown at AMD's Advancing AI 2026 event, is designed to run large language models entirely on a single machine without a discrete GPU.

The configuration marks the first time a mini-ITX desktop has shipped with 192 GB of unified memory, according to Notebookcheck, positioning Framework ahead of competitors in the emerging local AI hardware market.

Under the Hood

The Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 is an update to AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, retaining 16 Zen 5 CPU cores but raising the boost clock to 5.2 GHz. The integrated Radeon 8065S GPU packs 40 RDNA 3.5 Compute Units running at 3 GHz, making it AMD's fastest integrated graphics solution — capable of pushing AAA games at 1080p, according to Notebookcheck. An on-chip NPU delivers up to 55 TOPS for AI acceleration.

https://x.com/DigitalTrends/status/2080242255898751415

The 192 GB of unified LPDDR5X memory operates at 8,533 MT/s, delivering 273 GB/s of bandwidth. That represents a 50% capacity increase and a 6.6% bandwidth improvement over the MAX+ 395 system's 128 GB at 256 GB/s, according to Wccftech.

Framework says the memory is sufficient to run DeepSeek V4-Flash — a model with 284 billion total parameters and 13 billion active parameters — at Q8 quantization on a single box, with room to spare for additional context length. A Q8 GGUF build of the model occupies approximately 162 GB, according to VideoCardz.

Open-Ended PCIe and Cluster Potential

The updated Desktop replaces the previous PCIe x4 slot with an open-ended design, allowing physically larger PCIe cards to be installed even though they continue to operate through four lanes. To demonstrate the potential, Framework set up a proof-of-concept cluster using two 50 GbE network adapters with RDMA over Ethernet (RoCE). The setup connects two 192 GB systems and uses tensor parallelism to access a combined 384 GB of memory across both machines.

"Seize the means of computation."

— Framework, promotional tagline for the new Desktop

Framework also confirmed a pre-built version with a Linux distribution pre-loaded, expanding beyond the company's traditional DIY kit model.

Pricing Remains a Question Mark

Framework has not announced pricing or a release date for the 192 GB configuration. The company warned that rising LPDDR5X prices mean the new model will carry a "pretty substantial jump" over the current 128 GB Framework Desktop, which already costs $3,449 — up from $1,999 when the Desktop was first revealed in February 2025.

For context, NVIDIA's DGX Spark ships with 128 GB of LP5X memory and costs close to $5,000. Wccftech estimates the 192 GB Framework Desktop could exceed $5,000 when it reaches retail later this year. Framework is not alone in targeting this segment — GMKtec has confirmed an EVO-X3 configuration with the same processor and 192 GB of memory for later in 2026, according to VideoCardz.

What It Means for AI Developers

The 192 GB configuration addresses one of the biggest bottlenecks in local AI development: memory capacity. Running frontier-class models locally, without relying on cloud APIs, requires enough unified memory to hold the entire model in RAM. Until now, that typically meant spending upwards of $10,000 on workstation hardware or NVIDIA's server-grade systems.

A compact desktop that can fit a 284-billion-parameter model at high quantization could appeal to AI researchers, developers, and startups — particularly those looking to reduce cloud compute costs or keep data on-premises. For Indian tech professionals and AI startups, where data sovereignty concerns and cloud pricing are growing considerations, affordable local inference hardware represents a meaningful shift.
